title: Lock-Free Concurrent Queue Simulation
prompt:
Implement the Michael-Scott lock-free queue in Python using simulated compare-and-swap (CAS) semantics, with a deterministic concurrency test harness.

Part 1 — CAS SIMULATION:
Implement a simulated atomic CAS operation. Since Python's GIL makes true lock-free programming unnecessary, we simulate the concurrency model:

  class AtomicRef:
      def __init__(self, value):
          self.value = value
      def cas(self, expected, new_value) -> bool:
          """Atomically: if self.value is expected, set to new_value and return True; else return False."""

Use threading.Lock internally for the CAS simulation only. The queue algorithm itself must NOT use any locks — it must use only CAS operations.

Part 2 — MICHAEL-SCOTT QUEUE:
Implement the queue with:
  - A sentinel/dummy node (the queue always has at least one node).
  - enqueue(value): uses CAS on tail.next, then advances tail.
  - dequeue() -> value or None: uses CAS on head, skips the dummy node.
  - The tail-lagging case must be handled: if tail.next is not None, help advance tail before retrying enqueue.
  - dequeue must correctly handle the case where head == tail (queue appears empty but tail may be lagging).

Part 3 — TEST HARNESS:
Run 4 producer threads and 4 consumer threads concurrently:
  - Each producer enqueues 1000 values: producer i enqueues (i, 0), (i, 1), ..., (i, 999).
  - Each consumer dequeues until it has consumed 1000 values (busy-wait retry if queue is empty).
  - After all threads complete, verify:
    a. All 4000 values were dequeued (no lost values).
    b. No duplicate values were dequeued.
    c. Within each producer's values, the relative order is preserved (FIFO per producer).
    d. The queue is empty after all consumers finish.

Part 4 — ABA DEMONSTRATION:
Explain the ABA problem in the context of this queue. Show a specific interleaving of operations where ABA could cause incorrect behavior if CAS compared only pointer values (without a version counter or tagged pointer). Then explain why Python's object identity (the 'is' operator) naturally avoids ABA for newly allocated nodes.

Provide complete Python code for Parts 1-3 and a written explanation for Part 4. Show the test harness output demonstrating all four verification checks pass.
verification_method: Run the code. The test harness must complete without deadlock and pass all four checks: (1) exactly 4000 unique values dequeued, (2) no duplicates, (3) per-producer FIFO ordering preserved, (4) queue empty at end. The enqueue and dequeue methods must use only CAS operations (no locks in the queue logic itself). Verify that the tail-lagging case is handled in enqueue (look for the pattern: if tail.next is not None, CAS tail forward). Verify the dequeue handles head == tail correctly.
why_frontier_hard: The Michael-Scott queue has two subtle correctness issues that models frequently miss: (1) The tail-lagging case: after a successful CAS on tail.next, the enqueuing thread may be preempted before advancing tail. Other enqueuers must detect this and help advance tail. Models often omit this helping step, causing the queue to break under concurrency. (2) The dequeue of the dummy node: when head == tail and tail.next is not None, the queue has one real element but head points to the dummy. The dequeue must advance tail first (helping), then retry. Models commonly either return None incorrectly or skip the dummy node wrong. (3) The test harness with 4+4 threads exposes timing-dependent bugs that simpler tests miss.
ground_truth_notes: The Michael-Scott queue (1996) uses a dummy/sentinel node. Enqueue: allocate node, loop: read tail and tail.next. If tail.next is None, CAS tail.next to new node, then CAS tail to new node. If tail.next is not None, CAS tail to tail.next (help advance), retry. Dequeue: loop: read head, tail, head.next. If head == tail: if head.next is None, return None (empty); else CAS tail to head.next (help). If head != tail: read value from head.next, CAS head to head.next. The value comes from head.next, not head (head is the dummy). Python's object identity avoids ABA because each 'Node()' allocation creates a unique object.
